1	# Task 11: Solar-system explorer with focus on click
2	
3	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite, rendering to the canvas with id #app. The app is an interactive, stylised solar system explorer on a dark starfield background.
4	
5	Show a glowing central star and at least 6 planets, each at a different orbital distance, with a different size and colour and orbiting the star at a different speed (inner planets faster). At least one planet has a moon orbiting it, and at least one planet has a ring. Draw a thin circular orbit line for each planet. Planets should also spin about their own axis. Use a simple procedural look (colour, gradients or generated textures); do not load external assets from the network.
6	
7	The user can click a planet to focus on it. On focus, the camera smoothly moves (about 1.5 seconds, eased) to a close view of that planet and keeps following it as it orbits, and a DOM info panel appears showing the planet's name, its orbital period in Earth days, and its distance from the star in million km. Clicking empty space, or pressing the Escape key, smoothly returns to the overview showing the whole system and hides the panel. In the overview, the user can drag to orbit the camera around the system and scroll to zoom within sensible limits. Add a toggle button labelled 'Pause' that stops and resumes orbital motion, and shows 'Play' while paused.
8	
9	The scene must look correct on first load with no console errors. Expose

I'm leaning toward using app.camera?.setPose with a cut flag, though I'm wary it might get smoothed instead of applied immediately. I also need to handle the case where app.camera is undefined, since picking relies on my own projection which in turn depends on the camera's current pose being accessible.

For picking math, I'm working out how to convert pointer coordinates (using the canvas's bounding rect at 640x360) into view-space rays using the vertical field of view, and I'll distinguish clicks from drags by checking if movement stays under 4px.

For the planets, I'm deciding against uncertain material presets or procedural texture APIs and instead planning a custom GLSL shader with noise-based color bands, lit by a sun light direction computed from world position via the model matrix.

Writing shader code...

I'll add bloom for the sun's glow, since custom shaders don't need scene lights to render. For rings, rather than using a flattened cylinder (which just gives a solid disc), I'll build a plane and discard fragments outside a radius band based on local XZ position to carve out the ring shape.

Given uncertainty over whether unit primitives span ±0.5 or ±1, I decide to sidestep the ambiguity entirely by defining the ring geometry explicitly myself—a flat annulus mesh with 64 segments, inner/outer radius around 1.4–2.2 relative to the planet, double-sided, with colors derived from vertex position.

For orbit lines, I'm weighing options: a "lines" topology with paired indices feels risky since it might render nothing if unsupported and I'd have no way to verify, versus a thin flat ribbon annulus that stays visible from most angles but could vanish at grazing viewing angles. I lean toward trying the lines topology first but keep the ribbon approach as a fallback in case the material doesn't render.

For moons and rings, I'll compute world positions manually and set rotation via runtime handles, keeping the ring as a separate tilted node so it doesn't spin with the planet's axial rotation—just applying a constant tilt while the planet itself spins about its own axis.

Since banding patterns alone would look invariant to spin around the vertical axis, I need to add noise-based surface features like blobs and spots so the rotation is actually visible, using the local object-space position to drive both the latitude bands and the 3D noise. For the sun, I'm planning an emissive shader with noisy surface detail plus a separate larger halo sphere using fresnel-based additive transparency for the glow effect.

For the starfield, I'm setting a dark background color and scattering many tiny white sphere instances at a large radius, using a custom material that just outputs solid white color since lighting won't apply correctly to instanced stars.

Using plain boxes with an unlit shader keeps it simple since rotation and color tinting don't matter for tiny stars. For the camera, I'm setting up an orbit around the origin with yaw/pitch/distance parameters and a default overview angle, then planning eight planets with orbital radii spaced roughly from 16 to 93 units so the outer orbit still fits comfortably in view.

I'm computing the horizontal field of view to pick a sensible default distance (around 160) with clamped min/max zoom, then assigning realistic-ish sizes and orbital periods to each planet so their angular speeds scale correctly relative to each other.

Real orbital periods make Neptune's motion imperceptible, so instead of using literal day-ratios I'm devising a stylized visual period formula (scaling roughly with period^0.55) so outer planets still visibly crawl while inner ones noticeably zip around.

I'll stagger each planet's starting angle so they don't all line up, keep orbits flat in the XZ plane with y at zero, and have the pause control stop both orbital motion and spin together.

Simulation time advances only while unpaused, but camera easing keeps running during pause so it can still follow its target. For focus transitions, I'll animate the camera over 1.5 seconds with an easeInOutCubic curve, computing the end pose each frame from the planet's current position so the camera smoothly settles into an offset that blends radial direction and elevation, positioning it on the sun-facing side of the planet.

To actually see the lit side with some phase visible, I'm biasing the offset direction mostly radial toward the sun with a tangential component tied to orbit direction, plus a slight upward tilt—this way the camera orbits along with the planet while keeping a consistent relative view. I'll compute the camera distance directly from my own camera-to-planet position rather than relying on a stored value, since it naturally varies during the transition and settles at the intended focus distance once done.

For moons, I'm giving Earth one moon and Jupiter one, sized smaller than planets, with orbit radii chosen so they stay within the framing when focused. Saturn gets a tilted ring using a banded, semi-transparent double-sided shader. For planet picking, I'm switching to a ray-sphere intersection test using the camera's world-space ray and a slightly enlarged radius for forgiveness, picking the nearest hit, and accounting for how small distant planets like Mercury appear in the overview.

I'm computing a minimum pick radius based on world-space pixel size at the planet's distance so tiny distant planets remain clickable, then selecting whichever hit has the smallest ray distance. Clicking the sun or empty space unfocuses, clicking a new planet transitions focus to it, and clicking the already-focused planet does nothing. I'll make sure the picking ray uses the same pose and fov as the actual rendered camera so clicks line up with what's displayed.

For `__focusPlanet`, I need case-insensitive name matching that mirrors click behavior exactly, ignoring unknown names, with planet positions exposed as read-only frozen getters computed fresh each frame from live simulation state. I'm also handling the overview camera as an orbit around the origin with its own yaw/pitch/distance that resets to the last user orbit on unfocus, and making sure drag input is ignored during transitions unless already in overview mode.

I'm using performance.now() rather than accumulated frame dt for the transition timer, since clamped dt would stretch a 1.5s transition if the headless renderer runs at low framerate.

Linear position lerp from overview to close-up might pass through other bodies but that's acceptable to skip for now. I'm also wiring up escape key handling and a pause button fixed over the canvas, making sure pointer events only register on the canvas itself.
